bibliography.abstract: Roundabouts are widely recognized as effective intersection treatments for improving road safety. However, concerns remain regarding motorcyclist safety in mixed-traffic environments, particularly at roundabout entries where complex yielding and merging interactions occur. This study investigates motorcycle conflict severity at roundabout entries using surrogate safety analysis based on Post-Encroachment Time. Data were collected using unmanned aerial vehicles at four single-lane roundabouts in Khon Kaen University, Thailand. A total of 950 motorcycle entry interactions were extracted and classified into four severity levels: minor, moderate, severe, and critical. An ordered probit model was employed to identify the rider-, traffic-, and geometry-related factors associated with increasing conflict severity. The results indicate that passenger presence, yielding behavior, entry speed, conflict vehicle type, and radius of deflection significantly influence conflict severity. Among these factors, yielding behavior exhibited the strongest effect, highlighting the importance of compliance with entry priority rules. Interactions involving motorcycles were also associated with higher conflict severity than those involving passenger cars. Notably, among conventional geometric dimensions examined, only radius of deflection, which directly representing path curvature, remained significant. This finding suggests that path-based geometric measures may provide a more meaningful representation of motorcycle safety performance than conventional roundabout dimensions alone. Overall, the results indicate that motorcycle conflict severity at roundabout entries is governed primarily by rider behavior and traffic interactions, while effects of self-enforcing geometry appear to be expressed through rider speed control and trajectory adjustment. These findings highlight the importance of considering motorcycle-specific behavioral responses when evaluating roundabout safety in mixed-traffic environments.
bibliography.title: Motorcycle conflict severity at roundabout entries: the roles of rider behavior and self-enforcing geometry

en.caveats: The findings are based on a small sample of four roundabouts within a single university campus, which may limit generalizability to broader urban or highway environments.
en.what: This study analyzed 950 motorcycle entry interactions captured via unmanned aerial vehicles at four single-lane roundabouts in Khon Kaen University, Thailand. Using Post-Encroachment Time to measure surrogate safety, the researchers classified conflicts into four severity levels and used an ordered probit model to evaluate the influence of rider behavior, traffic conditions, and roundabout geometry. The analysis revealed that yielding behavior had the strongest impact on conflict severity, and that among geometric factors, only the radius of deflection significantly influenced safety outcomes.
en.why: It demonstrates that path-based geometric measures, specifically the radius of deflection, are more reliable indicators of motorcycle safety than traditional roundabout dimensions, showing that geometric design influences safety primarily by forcing riders to adjust their speed and trajectory.
